title: Instagram Edits uygulamasına içerik üreticileri için yapay zeka asistanı eklendi
summary: Meta, video düzenleme uygulaması Edits için hesap verilerini analiz eden yapay zeka tabanlı yeni bir asistan duyurdu.
body:
Instagram, içerik üreticilerinin hesap performansını analiz ederek kişiselleştirilmiş öneriler sunan yapay zeka destekli yeni asistanını tanıttı. Meta'nın TikTok'un uygulaması CapCut'a rakip olarak konumlandırdığı Edits uygulamasına eklenen bu araç, genel tavsiyeler yerine içerik üreticilerinin kendi verilerine odaklanıyor.

## Edits asistanı nasıl çalışıyor?

TechCrunch'ın aktardığına göre, asistan takipçi sayıları, izlenmeler, beğeniler, paylaşımlar ve video izlenme süreleri gibi hesap metriklerini güncel trendlerle birleştiriyor. Edits uygulamasının yöneticisi Brett Westervelt, aracın performans desenlerini zaman içinde tespit ederek ham metriklerden çıkarılması zor olan içgörüler sunduğunu belirtti. The Verge'ün haberine göre içerik üreticileri, asistanlığa trendler veya geçmiş videoların neden başarılı olduğu hakkında açık uçlu sorular sorabiliyor ve kanca cümleleri, altyazılar ya da ses parçaları için öneriler alabiliyor.

## Kullanım limitleri ve Meta One aboneliği

Engadget'ın haberine göre yeni asistan temel kullanım için ücretsiz sunuluyor ancak günlük bir sınır bulunuyor. Sınırı aşmak isteyen yoğun kullanıcıların daha yüksek kullanım limitlerinin kilidini açmak için bir Meta One aboneliği edinmesi gerekiyor. Meta, bu yapay zeka aracını ilk olarak haziran ayında özel bir etkinlikte önizlemişti.

**Neden önemli?** Platformların içerik üreticilerine doğrudan nasıl paylaşım yapacaklarına dair yönlendirmeler sunması, sosyal medya metrikleri ve algoritma ilişkisinde yeni bir döneme işaret ediyor.

source_texts.title: Instagram rolls out an AI video editor for creators
source_texts.summary: This conversational AI assistant is intended to provide personalized feedback to creators, rather than generic advice.
source_texts.text:
Instagram announced on Wednesday that it’s bringing an AI video editing tool to Edits, its CapCut competitor.
This conversational AI assistant is intended to provide personalized feedback to creators, rather than generic advice.
“The assistant knows your account’s Instagram metrics, things like follows, views, video retention, likes, shares and combines them with your comments, what’s trending on Instagram and what your audience is into,” Brett Westervelt, who leads the Edits app, said in a blog post. “It can spot patterns in your performance over time and surface actionable insights that are hard to see from the metrics alone.”
Westervelt added that Edits worked closely with a group of creators in developing the tool.
“One thing we heard consistently: creators want a tool that handles the analysis, not one that does the creative work for them,” he wrote. “Edits assistant does the digging for you. The creative calls are still yours.”
Meta first previewed the Edits AI assistant in June at an invite-only creator event, where it also said it was working on an Edits desktop app. It’s not the only company working on tools like this, though. YouTube announced last week that it is also working on a conversational video editing tool, which should be available early next year.
From what we can tell so far, it looks like Meta is taking a more analytics-driven approach with its AI assistant than YouTube, which suggested creators would use its AI to help with the actual editing process.
Creators will have a limit to how much they can use the AI tool, but they can unlock more usage with a Meta One subscription.

source_texts.text:
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.
Instagram is adding an AI ‘assistant’ to tell you how to post
What happens when platforms tell everyone how to optimize their content?
Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. The tool pulls in data and metrics such as likes, views, retention on videos, and shares. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos.
Are you a creator using platforms’ AI tools?
I want to hear from you about your experience. Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal.
If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.
It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? Is there no ceiling for the amount of time audiences are willing to spend on the platforms? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post?
The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. This, too, speaks to the changing winds: Meta needs to finance its lofty AI ambitions, and it’s already signaled that premium social media features may be part of how it does it. It’s not hard to imagine a future where meaningful feedback and AI-driven analytics and insights are for paying subscribers. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.

source_texts.title: Meta introduces a new AI assistant for its Instagram creators
source_texts.summary: The Edits assistant offers personalized guidance based on your audience and best-performing content.
source_texts.text:
Meta introduces a new AI assistant for its Instagram creators
The Edits assistant offers personalized guidance based on your audience and best-performing content.
It isn't hard to find AI-generated guidance for just about anything these days, but Meta thinks it has come up with the perfect solution for its extensive creator community with its new Edits assistant.
ICYMI, Edits is Meta's creator-focused video editing app, which it launched last year as a rival to TikTok's CapCut. The new Edits assistant is being pitched by Meta as a highly personalized chatbot that understands each individual's audience, rather than simply offering generic and, well, slop-adjacent AI advice.
In a press release, Meta said your new "creative partner" can analyze your insights and suggest video ideas based on previous content performance and current trends. You can ask it what videos have performed well for you recently, or for feedback on why some reels haven't resonated as much with your audience.
The assistant can dig into all of your Instagram data, including follows, views, likes, shares and retention stats, which it will draw on when responding to your prompts. It looks at patterns of performance rather than tailoring its advice to one video that has done big numbers, and will suggest concepts, hooks and captions for future videos based on how you've approached the platform in the past. It can also suggest what audio to use based on the style of content you make.
The Edits assistant has already been trialled by select creators in Meta's community, and it will be free to use in the app until you hit an unspecified daily prompt limit. The company will no doubt hope the new feature will push more creators into signing up for one of its new Meta One subscriptions, which will unlock higher usage limits for power users. The most expensive of these plans costs a whopping $499 per month.
